newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Copper steady, but vulnerable to Chinese rumours.
newsitem.headline: Copper steady, but vulnerable to Chinese rumours.

text.p: Copper prices on the London Metal Exchange (LME) are expected to be supported at current levels on Thursday, but could be vulnerable to rumours of China's plans to sell some of its reserves, Far East traders said.

Since the beginning of the week, the market has been swirling with rumours, denied by China's Central Reserve Bureau, that Beijing was preparing to exploit high world prices by selling copper on the LME, the dealers said.
"If there are no Chinese copper sales, copper prices will get some support at around the level of around US$2,470 a tonne," said a metal trader in Seoul.
Three-month copper was quoted in thin Asian trade at $2,467/72 a tonne at 0615 GMT, slightly down from Wednesday's late LME close of $2,467/71 a tonne.
A recent decline in the copper market was mainly due to a correction to ease a technically overbought situation, one dealer said. He pegged resistance for three-month copper at $2,550.
Another trader said the strike at Inco Ltd. had failed to boost copper prices, but had provided a support level.
Inco's Sudbury complex, where workers have been on strike since Tuesday, produces about 90,000 tonnes of copper annually and helps to supply the Northeast and Midwest U.S. markets.

A trader with POSCO, South Korea's largest steel maker, said nickel prices were likely to slide further due to weak seasonal demand and the continued high use of secondary nickel by stainless steel producers.
"Demand is normally shrinking in the third quarter due to the summer holiday," the POSCO trader said.
The trader said steel makers were shutting down for two or three weeks in the third quarter for their holidays.
He pegged support for three-month nickel at $6,800 a tonne and resistance at $7,200.
"Except for strike-hit Inco, most producers are in full operation," he said, adding a longer strike at Inco may eventually impact on the nickel market.
